doc.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Syndication through TCB and other jazz filmmakers
summary: Crohn explains how a syndicator sold jazz film packages and names Bruce Ricker and Don McGlynn as filmmakers to interview.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Oh, yeah. Do you think people get the wrong idea, like oh you’re making a film, you’re going to make a lot of money on your film — I said a joke didn’t I?

Well yes and no. First of all, there are exceptions to every rule. And you know I’m crying poor here, but there was a period in my life when I did the “History of Jazz” series, there was a market for jazz films. And I had what they call a syndicator in England. He had a company called TCB, meaning taking care of business. His name was Angus Trowbridge — it’s a great British name — but he was an American and he lived outside of London. And he would go around to Cannes and different names of film festivals where buyers come, TV sent representatives and they come, and they buy. So he would only have jazz films. That’s what TCB was about. And he had these whole bunch of jazz films and he’d sell a package: okay you have two of Burrill’s films and three of this film and three of that film, and you’d buy the whole package. And then he would sell it, he’d take twenty- five percent for himself, and he’d send checks. And they would come in the mail. That was great. So I got paid for doing the film, and then we got paid afterwards. So nowadays — and of course there are always people like Ken Burns — Ken Burns makes money when he does — he makes money whatever he does. And I also mentioned, when you first contacted me, about being the first person, as a jazz filmmaker, I said I’m not the first person you should be interviewing. The first one is Bruce Ricker, who did “Last of the Blue Devils” and then he went on to become friends with Clint Eastwood. He did “Straight, No Chaser,” and he did a wonderful film on Louie Prima, and he did one on Harold Arlen and he did some beautiful films, and he made money from doing them. And then there’s Don McGlynn who’s probably the most prolific jazz filmmaker, “Mingus” and — oh I take it back, I take it back — it’s Don McGlynn who did Louie Prima and Harold Arlen and Mingus and Horace Parlan and Howlin’ Wolf. But Bruce did a couple of American Masters — he did one on Tony Bennett, that’s what he did, a really good film on Tony Bennett. So Don McGlynn and Bruce Ricker both did okay in jazz, and Don is very much alive and very prolific and still making films. He is a very good person to go talk to. And Don is a true film buff. He can talk about films for hours. He’s very

knowledgeable. He’s just a good guy all around and he’s been very prolific. And he always finds money to make films. I don’t think he makes a lot of money when he makes them, but then the TV sales and — well you’d have to talk to him. I don’t know what his economic thing is.
